name: Virginia
overview: Virginia does not sell tax liens; a city or county sells the delinquent real estate itself through a court case. The locality's tax-collecting officer (usually the treasurer) can start a judicial proceeding once taxes are still delinquent on December 31 following the second anniversary of the date they became due (sooner for some derelict or blighted property). The case runs in the circuit court of the locality, and the property is sold at a judicial sale. The owner can redeem before the date set for the sale by paying into court all taxes, penalties and interest, plus costs including publication and a reasonable attorney fee set by the court.

counties.office: Chesterfield County Treasurer's Office (judicial sales handled by the county's attorney, James W. Elliott, and a court-appointed special commissioner of sale)
counties.address: 9901 Lori Road, Chesterfield, VA 23832 (mailing: P.O. Box 70, Chesterfield, VA 23832)
counties.next_sale_note: No sale date is posted on the county page; it says the attorney typically advertises each sale in the newspaper.
counties.how_to_bid: The county refers qualified properties to its attorney, and the Circuit Court appoints a special commissioner of sale, who may sell by private bid, public auction (held on the steps of the County Courthouse) or a listing with a real estate agent. A minimum deposit based on a percentage of the bid price may be required on the sale date, with the balance due within a set time. Property is sold as is; buyers pay for title searches, recording costs and grantor's tax, and bids that do not cover the taxes and sale costs may be rejected. Registration steps are not stated; call the attorney for sale details.
